John F. Kennedy. On June 26, 1963, the president traveled to West Berlin, where he stood at the Rudolph Wilde Platz at the height of Cold War tensions. He had come to express American solidarity with the divided city and reaffirm the West's commitment to resisting Soviet expansion.

Sixteen months earlier, in August 1961, the Berlin Wall had been constructed, physically dividing the city. Now Kennedy spoke directly to that division. He acknowledged the difficulties of freedom—democracy was not perfect, he said, but free people told of their failures and learned from them, whereas dictatorships merely boasted of their accomplishments. Then he made his decisive declaration, speaking in halting German: "Ich bin ein Berliner." I am a Berliner. The crowd of approximately 450,000 roared approval.

That simple statement, spoken in German, electrified the trapped city by claiming solidarity across the ideological divide. Kennedy's words became an enduring symbol of the West's commitment to freedom. Delivered mere months before his assassination, his declaration that American power would protect freedom proved to be among his most resonant acts.
